No. 25-580
In the Supreme Court of the United States


GARY RICHARD WHITTON, PETITIONER,
v.

SECRETARY, FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS,
RESPONDENT.


ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE ELEVENTH CIRCUIT


BRIEF OF RETIRED JUDGES AS AMICI CURIAE
IN SUPPORT OF PETITIONER


CATHERINE WOOLLEY

(I)
QUESTIONS PRESENTED
1. Whether in determining whether a constitutional error had a prejudicial effect on the outcome of a trial a
court must consider only that evidence that was presented
to the jury at the trial.
2. Whether the prejudice from the Giglio  violation in
this case met the standards for relief under Giglio  and
Brecht.

INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici curiae  are former federal and state judges
with decades of combined experience on the bench. 2
Amici have devoted much of their professional lives to
improving the justice system .  As relevant here, a mici
maintain a continuing interest in ensuring that the rules
governing criminal proceedings are both administrable by
courts and protective of the constitutional rights of
defendants.  Based on their deep experience as judges at
both the trial and appellate levels, amici submit this brief
to emphasize that the rule adopted by the Eleventh
Circuit in the decision below is unworkable in practice.
Permitting the introduction of post-trial evidence into the
post-conviction prejudice analyses would invite extensive
speculation and inject unpredictability into the criminal
legal system.  Amici believe these considerations take on
a heightened importance in the context of capital cases ,
where courts must decide whether a person can legally be
put to death by the State.
Amici are:
Judge Mark. W. Bennett (Ret.) —District Judge
(1994-2015), Chief Judge (2000-2007), Senior Judge (2015-
2019) for the United States District Court for the
Northern District of Iowa; Magistrate Judge (1991 -1994)
for the United States District Court for the Southern
District of Iowa.
Judge LaDoris Hazzard Cordell (Ret.)—Judge

3


SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
In the decision below, the Eleventh Circuit held that
a court assessing prejudice may rely on post-verdict
evidence that the jury never saw  and no trial judge ever
admitted.  In so holding, the Eleventh Circuit has
required judges considering a post -conviction motion to
effectively conduct a  retrial.  And in that hypothetical
retrial, the court must not only  estimate the persuasive
value of post -verdict evidence but also imag ine how its
hypothetical admission would have altered every aspect of
the original trial.
By adopting this rule, the Eleventh Circuit asks
judges to do the impossible: to assess the credibility and
weight of evidence without any procedural safeguards, to
reconstruct counterfactual trials that never occurred
based on post -verdict evidence, and to predict the
reactions of juries to these hypoth etical trials while
lacking any principled way to account for the complex
human dynamics that shape verdicts.  The guesswork
mandated by the Eleventh Circuit’s rule is the opposite of
the clear rules that pr omote fair and efficient criminal
trials.  Indeed, g iven that the Eleventh Circuit’s rule
relies on extensive and layered speculation, arbitrary
outcomes are inevitable.   That is particularly true in the
context of capital cases, where the Eleventh Circuit’s rule
is likely to require judges to assess the credibility of everevolving forensic techniques based on little  more than
their own intuition.
The Eleventh Circuit also fails to provide any limiting
principle on parties’ ability to proffer post- verdict
evidence or any standards to guide a judge’s
determination of which pieces of post- evidence will be
admitted into the prejudice analysis.  This
unpredictability is e specially intolerable in capital cases,
where error is irrevocable and the Constitution demands

4


heightened care.  See Gregg v. Georgia, 428 U.S. 153, 187
(1976) (plurality opinion) (“When a defendant’s life is at
stake, the Court has been particularly sensitive to insure
that every safeguard is observed.”); Zant v. Stephens, 462
U.S. 862, 885 (1983) (“[T]he severity of the [capital]
sentence mandates careful scrutiny in the review of any
colorable claim of error.”).   The Eleventh Circuit’s
unworkable rule risks  undermining the consistency and
fairness of the criminal justice system when the stakes are
at their highest.
This Court has repeatedly rejected proposed rules of
criminal procedure as “[un]acceptable” when they “would
lead . . . to an unworkable standard.”  Montejo v.
Louisiana, 556 U.S. 778, 783 (2009); s ee also Arizona v.
Roberson, 486 U.S. 675, 680 (1988) (“[o]ne of the principal
advantages” of a rule of criminal procedure “is the ease
and clarity of its application”).   It should do so again in
this case by granting the petition for a writ of certiorari
and reversing the Eleventh Circuit’s decision.
ARGUMENT
THE RULE ADOPTED BY THE ELEVENTH CIRCUIT IS
UNWORKABLE
A. The Eleventh Circuit’s Rule Requires Judges to Make
Unreliable Determinations About Post-Verdict
Evidence
When it comes to the admission of evidence in a
criminal proceeding, procedure matters.  As amici can
attest, a lthough judges are trained in the rules of
evidence, “a mere judicial determination regarding the
reliability of evidence is no substitute for the
constitutionally prescribed method of assessing
reliability.”  Hemphill v. New York , 595 U.S. 140, 152
(2022) (quotations omitted) .  Our system of criminal
justice is in many ways built around the notion that

5


adversarial testing “beats and bolts out the Truth much
better” than mere judicial instinct.  M. Hale, History and
Analysis of the Common Law of England 258 (1713) .
Consistent with that principle, th is Court has rejected
arguments that constitutional safeguards around the
admission of evidence can be disregarded in the name of
efficiency, irrespective of how reliable the evidence may
appear.  See, e.g., Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts, 557
U.S. 305, 317-18 (2009) (quotations omitted) (“Dispensing
with confrontation because testimony is obviously reliable
is akin to dispensing with jury trial because a defendant is
obviously guilty.  This is not what the Sixth Amendment
prescribes.”).
The Eleventh Circuit’s rule makes precisely that kind
of impermissible tradeoff.  It circumvents the adversarial
procedures prescribed by the Constitution  and replac es
them with unguided judicial judg ement, all for the
apparent sake of avoiding additional proceedings during
a remand.  Judges will have to determine the credibility
and weight of post- verdict evidence in a procedural
vacuum, free of the array of procedural rules meticulously
followed at trial to create the universe of facts.
This case illustrates the problems with the Eleventh
Circuit’s novel approach.  Respondents introduced new
forensic evidence that retested the blood on Petitioner’s
boots more than a decade after Petitioner’s conviction.
The Eleventh Circuit relied on that forensic evidence to
conclude that the use of a perjured confession at
Petitioner’s trial was harmless.  Yet the allegedly critical
forensic evidence was never admitted into evidence by
any court.  And for the same reason, it was never
subjected to the crucible of adversarial testing at any
point.
Those departures from the standard evidentiary
process raise serious concerns about the reliability of the

6


evidence that formed the core of the Eleventh Circuit’s
prejudice analysis.  A s this Court has recognized,
“[f]orensic evidence is not uniquely immune from the risk
of manipulation. ” Melendez-Diaz, 557 U.S . at  318.
Indeed, “[b]ecause forensic scientists often are driven in
their work by a need to answer a particular question
related to the issues of a particular case, they sometimes
face pressure to sacrifice appropriate methodology for the
sake of expediency.”   Id. (citing National Research
Council of the  National Academies, Strengthening
Forensic Science in the United States: A Path Forward
23-24 (2009)).  And even a well-intended forensic analysis
may have serious methodological deficiencies ; errors,
intentional or other wise, are bound to occur.   It is in
recognition of these unavoidable pitfalls that our criminal
justice system subjects even arguably empirical,
“objective” evidence to the adversarial process .  But the
Eleventh Circuit rejected the wisdom of this
Constitutional design when it deemed itself capable of
assessing Respondent’s new forensic analysis without the
aid of any checks of the adversarial process.
The same concerns apply to the use of other forms of
post-verdict evidence in prejudice analyses.  In all cases,
judges will have to assess post -verdict evidence with no
established standards or procedures.   If a party
introduces new expert testimony, a judge will have to
assess the expert’s  credibility and subject matter
expertise without the Daubert  hearing and cross -
examination that would otherwise allow the opposing
party to excavate the expert’s bias, unreliability, or lack
of credibility.  Melendez-Diaz, 557 U.S. at 320 (noting that
an expert’s  “lack of proper training or deficiency in
judgment may be disclosed in cross -examination”).  If a
party introduces a  new affidavit, a judge will have to
assess the testimony therein without any of the additional
context generated by cross-examination.

7


Barred from utilizing  the typical tools and checks of
the fact- finding process, judges  run the risk of making
determinations about post-verdict evidence that lack a
credible foundation .  This is especially troubling in the
context of federal habeas capital cases.  This Court has
long acknowledged that “[t]here is no question that death,
as a punishment, is unique in its severity and
irrevocability.  When a defendant’s life is at stake, the
Court has been particularly sensitive to ensure that every
safeguard is observed.”  Gregg, 428 U.S. at 187 (plurality)
(citations omitted).  Forced to assess and weigh new postverdict evidence without any  procedural safeguards,
judges will be left searching in the dar k when reviewing
“the gravest sentence our society may impose” on a
person.  Hall v. Florida, 572 U.S. 701, 724 (2014).
B. The Eleventh Circuit’s R ule Requires Judges to
Conduct Counterfactual Mini -Trials Involving the
Parties’ New Evidence
The Eleventh Circuit’s rule further complicates
matters by  requiring judges to  predict how the
hypothetical admission of post-verdict evidence would
have impacted the original trial.  In other words, not only
will a judge have to speculate on the persuasive power of
the post -verdict evidence, but she will also have to ask
numerous “what if” questions to assess how the rest of the
trial would have unfolded after the admission of the new
evidence.  This is plainly unworkable.
Consider, for example, the introduction of a new
witness’ affidavit by the State .  Initially, a judge would
have to evaluate how persuasive the witness ’s testimony
would have been when initially presented to the jury.
That assessment includes speculating about the strength
of the witness’s testimony, while also considering any
supporting exhibits and demonstratives that the State
claims it would have introduced through the new witness.

8


Then, the judge would have to imagine how defense
counsel would have responded to the new evidence.  What
would have been the substance of the cross-examination,
and how successful would it have been?  Would  the
defendant have introduced additional witnesses in
response to the State’s witness’s testimony ?  A nd if so,
would those witnesses have been impeached or otherwise
discredited on cross-examination?
Beyond these complicated and potentially
unanswerable questions, a prudent judge would also have
to imagine how defense counsel might have restructured
their theory of the case in response to the new  evidence.
For instance, if the new witness purports to have seen the
defendant commit the crime, would the defendant have
conceded the offense but argued mitigation?  Or would the
defendant have opted to deny any role in the crime and
attack the witness’s testimony?  Even for a routine crime,
a judge would likely struggle to work through all the
permutations required by the Eleventh Circuit’s rule.
Such speculation is all the more challenging in the context
of a capital case, where the trial record is likely to be
lengthy and the jury is required to make determinations
beyond simple guilt or innocence.
At bottom,  the Eleventh Circuit’s rule ignores the
reality the even the most skilled and experienced  judge
cannot retrospectively invent the live courtroom context
that would have accompanied the introduction of the
evidence during trial .  For example, j urors and judges
frequently use nonverbal cues, such as eye contact, facial
expressions, and gestures, to assess counsel and witness
credibility.  Laurie L. Levenson, Courtroom Demeanor:
The Theater of the Courtroom , 92 Minn. L. Rev. 573, 582
(2008).  Indeed, the notion that courtroom demeanor is
important in deciding witness credibility is entrenched in
American jurisprudence.  Mark W. Bennett, Unspringing

9


the Witness Memory and Demeanor Trap, 64 Am. U. L.
Rev. 1331, 1346 (2015); see also Fed. R. Evid. Art. VIII
Advisory Committee Notes (“The demeanor of the
witness traditionally has been believed to furnish trier
and opponent with valuable clues.”); Olin Guy Wellborn
III, Demeanor, 76 Cornell L. Rev. 1075, 1104 (1991) (“The
notion that viewing the appearance and demeanor of a
witness significantly assists a trier of fact to determine
the truthfulness of the witness ’s testimony appears to be
as ancient as tes timony itself.”) .  Any single comment,
gesture, or impression made by a witness could change a
trial in ways small or large.  Under the Eleventh Circuit’s
rule, however, judges will have to make predictions while
reviewing evidence devoid of the live context that would
have accompanied its hypothetical introduction.
C. The Eleventh Circuit’s R ule Will Produce
Inconsistent Outcomes in Similar Cases
Predictability and uniformity are  essential to a fair
criminal legal system.  See Davis v. United States , 160
U.S. 469, 488 (1895) (explaining that “it is desirable that
there be uniformity of rule in the administration of the
criminal law”).  A prejudice analysis that permits the kind
of extensive and layered speculation  called for by the
Eleventh Circuit undermines those twin aims.  Because
imagining a counterfactual trial based on post- verdict
evidence is an entirely subjective practice, different
judges will naturally come to different conclusions.  T he
incorporation of post-verdict evidence with no procedural
guardrails or limiting principles will thus inevitably
produce arbitrary outcomes.
This Court has already recognized the pitfalls of rules
that permit judges to “a ttach[] the same significance to
opposite facts.”  Crawford v. Washington, 541 U.S. 36, 63
(2004).  In Crawford, for example, the Court held that the
nine-factor Roberts test for reliability was “so

10


unpredictable that it fail [ed] to provide meaningful
protection from even core confrontation violations. ”  Id.
The Court provided several examples to demonstrate that
“[w]hether a statement is deemed reliable depends
heavily on which factors the judge considers and how
much weight he accords each of them.”  Id.
That rationale applies with equal force here: a judge’s
prediction about the impact of post- verdict evidence
depends heavily, and impermissibly, on the factors the
judge considers and t he weight that individual jurist
accords each of them.   One judge may find a statement
made by a witness in custody more persuasive to a
hypothetical jury because the statement was clearly
against the witness’s penal interest.  A nother judge may
find a witness’s statement more persuasive because the
witness was not a suspect or in custody.  See id.  One judge
may find a forensic analysis conducted the day of the
crime more persuasive because of its immediacy.  Another
judge may find a forensic analysis conducted years later
more persuasive on the assumption that more recent
methodologies tend to be more advanced.  The rampant
unpredictability that would result from the Eleventh
Circuit’s rule is an “unpardonable vice” —especially in
capital cases where a defendant’s life hangs in the balance.
Id. at 63.
Moreover, the Eleventh Circuit proposes no limiting
principle for its  rule, thereby inviting selective
incorporation of post-verdict evidence.  Again, this case is
a perfect example: t he Eleventh Circuit embraced
inculpatory postconviction evidence offered by the State
without incorporating any of the exculpatory  evidence
defense counsel had uncovered since Petitioner’s trial.  It
is untenable to expect judges  to incorporate unlimited
additional post-verdict evidence into a prejudice analysis;
accordingly, judges will be forced  to employ their own

11


discretion, unguided by any uniform standards, to
determine which pieces of post- verdict evidence will be
incorporated.  I n practice, then, the Eleventh Circuit’s
rule imposes several layers of arbitrariness: first in the
threshold decision of what post- verdict evidence will be
incorporated into the prejudice analysis , and then in the
assessment of the evidence’s persuasiveness and  its
hypothetical impact on a trial .  That result would be
untenable in a routine criminal case.  It is unthinkable in
the context of a capital case like this one.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, amici respectfully submit
that the Court should grant the petition for certiorari and
reverse the decision of the Eleventh Circuit.

       Respectfully submitted,
